summary:
Colossae was a small city in the Lycus Valley of Asia Minor, and Paul had never been there; the church was planted by his coworker Epaphras. Word reached Paul in prison of a local teaching whose exact shape scholars still debate — some blend of law-keeping, ascetic rules, visions, and reverence for angelic powers — but whose effect was plain: it treated Christ as one spiritual power among many. This short letter is the rebuttal, sent together with the letter to Philemon (Onesimus, at the center of that letter, travels with both).

Paul answers with a hymn (1:15-20) containing the largest claims about Jesus in his letters: "the image of the invisible God," the one through whom and for whom all things were created. "He is before all things, and in Him all things hold together" (1:17). Chapter 2 draws the conclusion for the Colossians' situation: since "in Christ all the fullness of the Deity dwells in bodily form" (2:9), believers lack nothing and need no added rituals, visions, or restrictions to reach God. The rival regulations look wise, Paul says, and add nothing.

Chapters 3-4 apply it: set your minds on things above, strip off the old habits, put on compassion and patience, and let love bind the household together. The logic runs one direction the whole way, from who Christ is to how to live, and following that movement is the simplest way to read the letter.
